clue.text: Where novel needs plot, political novel needs this?

definitions.text: Where novel needs plot, political novel needs this?

parts.words: Where novel needs plot, political novel needs this?
parts.note: a plot is both a story line and a secret scheme; a political thriller needs a scheme of the second kind

explanation.surface: A piece of advice on writing fiction: every novel needs a plot, and a political novel needs something more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' has two senses: the storyline every novel needs, and the secret scheme that drives a political thriller.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot in the sense of a secret scheme by several people is a synonym.

clue.text: Old king of political economy?

explanation.surface: A question about a former monarch with an interest in economics.
explanation.walkthrough: Old King Cole is the 'merry old soul' of the nursery rhyme; G. D. H. Cole was an English political economist and historian.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery-rhyme monarch shares his name with the Oxford economist G. D. H. Cole.

clue.text: Nobody can identify submarine skipper

explanation.surface: A remark that no one can say who commands a submarine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin word for 'nobody' is also the name of Jules Verne's captain of the submarine Nautilus.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for no one, and the captain of Verne's Nautilus in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.

clue.text: Possibly no marital hop would be complete without it?

definitions.text: Possibly no marital hop would be complete without it?

indicators.note: 'possibly' says these letters could be arranged another way, so they are shuffled

explanation.surface: A suggestion that a wedding dance is incomplete without some extra item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' shuffles NO MARITAL HOP; the whole clue also defines Spenser's wedding song, which belongs before any marriage celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser's Prothalamion is a song celebrating a forthcoming marriage, so a wedding would be incomplete without such a poem.

clue.text: Poe's bells kept time in this sort of rhyme

definitions.text: Poe's bells kept time in this sort of rhyme

parts.words: Poe's bells kept time in this sort of rhyme
parts.note: recalls the line in Poe's poem The Bells about keeping time in a sort of ancient Norse rhyme

explanation.surface: A literary note on the rhythm of Edgar Allan Poe's poem about bells.
explanation.walkthrough: Poe's The Bells has the lines 'Keeping time, time, time, / In a sort of Runic rhyme'.
explanation.definitionFit: Poe's own phrase in The Bells describes the rhyme as of the old Germanic-alphabet kind.

clue.text: Eponymous features by Compton Mackenzie and Edith Wharton amount to miles of dead creatures in Australia

definitions.text: miles of dead creatures in Australia

parts.note: Coral is the title heroine of Compton Mackenzie's 1925 novel of that name
Edith Wharton wrote the novel The Reef, whose title feature it is

explanation.surface: Title subjects of two novels add up to a vast stretch of dead marine life off Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: Each piece is the thing a novel is named after: Mackenzie's Coral and Wharton's The Reef. The Great Barrier Reef is built from the skeletons of dead polyps.
explanation.definitionFit: A reef off Queensland stretches for many miles and is made of the skeletons of dead polyps.

clue.text: "As it-, it ain't. That's logic" (Lewis Carroll)

definitions.text: "As it-, it ain't. That's logic" (Lewis Carroll)

parts.words: "As it-, it ain't. That's logic" (Lewis Carroll)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Tweedledee in Through the Looking-Glass

explanation.surface: A quotation from Lewis Carroll with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Tweedledee says: 'if it was so, it might be; and if it were so, it would be; but as it isn't, it ain't. That's logic.'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the contraction of 'is not' in Tweedledee's speech.

clue.text: It "is an Impressionist painting", said Trevor. "It should be an explosion of truth"

definitions.text: It "is an Impressionist painting", said Trevor. "It should be an explosion of truth"

parts.words: It "is an Impressionist painting", said Trevor. "It should be an explosion of truth"
parts.note: William Trevor's description of the form of fiction he was most famous for writing

explanation.surface: A quotation from the Irish writer William Trevor about an art form.
explanation.walkthrough: William Trevor, the Irish writer best known for brief fiction, described the form as 'an Impressionist painting' and 'an explosion of truth'.
explanation.definitionFit: Trevor was describing the brief prose tale, the form he mastered.

clue.text: Ronald Harwood's kitchen piece?

explanation.surface: A question about a piece of kitchen furniture belonging to the playwright Ronald Harwood.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronald Harwood's play is about a dresser, the assistant who helps an actor into costume; a dresser is also a kitchen cabinet with shelves for plates.
explanation.definitionFit: Harwood's 1980 play about an actor's valet, and a kitchen sideboard with shelves for crockery.

clue.text: Oral eponym, perhaps, suggesting personal satire

indicators.note: 'perhaps' suggests the letters might form something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A word named after a man famous for slips of the tongue hints at mocking satire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oral eponym' looks like a description of Spooner, whose name gives an oral slip; it is anagram fodder for 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lampoonery is satire aimed at ridiculing a particular person.

clue.text: Money for old Hamilton work easily earned?

definitions.text: Money for old Hamilton work easily earned?

parts.words: Money for old Hamilton work easily earned?
parts.note: the idiom for easy money, 'money for old ...', with the gap filled by the title of a play by Patrick Hamilton

explanation.surface: A question whether the payment for an old work by Hamilton was easy money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Money for old rope' is a British idiom for money earned with no effort; Patrick Hamilton's play Rope was later filmed by Hitchcock.
explanation.definitionFit: Patrick Hamilton's play title completes the idiom for money gained with little effort.

clue.text: Waugh protagonist offering small change with a light touch

parts.note: a penny is a coin of small value
a feather gives the lightest of touches

explanation.surface: An Evelyn Waugh hero who gives out coins with delicacy.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Pennyfeather is the hero of Evelyn Waugh's Decline and Fall.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Pennyfeather is the central character of Waugh's novel Decline and Fall.

clue.text: The colonel, reader of Fowles book

parts.note: a lector is someone who reads aloud, as in church or at a university

explanation.surface: A military officer reading a novel by John Fowles.
explanation.walkthrough: A LECTOR reads the lessons in church, or is a university lecturer in some countries.
explanation.definitionFit: John Fowles's first novel, about a kidnapper who collects butterflies, has this title.

clue.text: Elegant sin wrongly identified with Shelley's lush roses

indicators.note: 'wrongly' says the letters are set in an incorrect order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Graceful wickedness mistakenly linked with Shelley's luxuriant roses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrongly' shuffles ELEGANT SIN. Eglantine, the sweet-briar, is a wild rose praised by the Romantic poets.
explanation.definitionFit: Eglantine is the sweet-briar, a fragrant wild rose often found in English poetry.

clue.text: One more competent expires outside, due to knavish tricks

indicators.note: 'outside' says the word for dying wraps round the other pieces

parts.note: to expire is to die
more competent means abler
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Someone more capable dies, and it is put down to devilish pranks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' puts ABLER and I inside DIES, split after DI.
explanation.definitionFit: Diableries are devilish deeds or mischief, from the French for devil.

clue.text: Lake surrounded by cunning wavy ornamental border

indicators.note: 'surrounded by' says the lake word is enclosed by the word for cunning

parts.note: cunning means guile
a loch is a Scottish lake

explanation.surface: A lake ringed by a crafty wavy decorative edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surrounded by' puts LOCH, the Scottish word for a lake, inside GUILE.
explanation.definitionFit: Guilloche is an architectural ornament of interlaced curving bands.

clue.text: Keyboard instrument comes with fashionable interior for Bentley domestic

indicators.note: 'interior' says the fashionable word sits inside the instrument

parts.note: a celeste is a keyboard instrument with hammers striking metal plates
in means fashionable

explanation.surface: A keyboard instrument with a trendy inside, made for a servant in a Bentley book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interior' puts IN inside CELESTE. Célestine is the French maid in E. C. Bentley's detective novel Trent's Last Case; 'Bentley' suggests the car.
explanation.definitionFit: Célestine is the maid in E. C. Bentley's Trent's Last Case.

clue.text: Dostoevsky's jottings on the Tube?

parts.note: Dostoevsky's ... from Underground, with London's Underground called the Tube

explanation.surface: A question about what Dostoevsky scribbled while riding the London Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tube is London's Underground railway, so jottings on it would be from the Underground, as in Dostoevsky's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Jottings are brief written memoranda, the word in Dostoevsky's title.

clue.text: Repository for Elia's poems

parts.note: Elia was the pen name of Charles Lamb, who wrote verses for friends' keepsake books

explanation.surface: A storage place for the verse of Charles Lamb.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Lamb wrote as 'Elia'; his 1830 Album Verses were poems written for friends' keepsake books.
explanation.definitionFit: A blank book for keeping verses, autographs or pictures is a repository of that kind.

clue.text: May it be with John Tanner, thought Shaw

definitions.text: May it be with John Tanner, thought Shaw

parts.words: May it be with John Tanner, thought Shaw
parts.note: echoes the blessing 'May the force be with you', with John Tanner the hero of Shaw's Man and Superman

explanation.surface: Shaw wishing something well for his character John Tanner.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shaw's Man and Superman, John Tanner is driven by the vital urge that propels evolution; the clue echoes 'May the force be with you' from Star Wars.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's term for the creative evolutionary drive that animates his hero.

clue.text: Let slip by Forsyth

parts.note: Antony's 'Cry havoc and let slip ...' in Julius Caesar, which also gave Frederick Forsyth a title

explanation.surface: Something accidentally revealed by the novelist Frederick Forsyth.
explanation.walkthrough: In Julius Caesar Antony cries 'havoc' and lets slip the animals of battle; Frederick Forsyth took the phrase for his 1974 mercenary thriller.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's phrase for the forces of battle unleashed, used as the title of a Forsyth thriller.

clue.text: Clown is second in gala

indicators.note: 'in' says the second goes inside the gala word

parts.note: a fete is a festive gala

explanation.surface: A jester comes second in a festival.
explanation.walkthrough: Feste is the jester in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night.
explanation.definitionFit: Feste is the fool in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night.

clue.text: Norse peer

parts.note: not a Scandinavian nobleman but the title character of Ibsen's play, whose first name is Peer

explanation.surface: A Scandinavian nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a noble; it is the first name of Ibsen's Norwegian hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibsen's verse play is named after its Norwegian hero, whose first name is Peer.

clue.text: William Morris's lacked provenance

parts.note: Morris's utopian romance title says its subject came from nowhere, that is, had no provenance

explanation.surface: Something owned by William Morris had no known origin.
explanation.walkthrough: William Morris wrote the utopian novel News from Nowhere; coming 'from nowhere' is lacking provenance.
explanation.definitionFit: Morris's book title News from Nowhere describes reports with no place of origin.

clue.text: Primitive from China, I fancy

indicators.note: 'from' says the answer is taken out of the letters of the following words

explanation.surface: A primitive-style artwork imported from China that the speaker likes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' takes the letters out of CHINA I FANCY.
explanation.definitionFit: A naïf is an artist in the untrained, primitive style.

clue.text: She's my nice new heroine, subject to Grant

indicators.note: 'new' says the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A speaker introduces a charming new heroine who is under the control of someone called Grant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' shuffles SHE'S MY NICE.
explanation.definitionFit: A heroine of a novel by Grant Allen is this young woman.

clue.text: American in 7 is hero of 1925 German novel

indicators.note: 'in' says the American abbreviation sits inside the letters from 7

parts.note: the answer to 7 down is two words whose initials are S and S

explanation.surface: An American inside a cross-reference turns out to be the hero of a German novel of 1925.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts US inside SS, the initials of the two-word answer at 7 down. Jud Süss is Lion Feuchtwanger's 1925 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Süss is the title figure of Lion Feuchtwanger's 1925 novel Jud Süss.

clue.text: Pompey supporter gives 'em net scare, perhaps

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the letters might be arranged another way, so they are shuffled

explanation.surface: A follower of Pompey gives his enemies a fright with a net.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' shuffles 'EM NET SCARE. Menecrates is one of Pompey's followers in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra.
explanation.definitionFit: Menecrates is a follower of Sextus Pompeius in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra.
